5|Requests HTTP Authentication and Redirect Test Community|"# Requests HTTP Authentication and Redirect Test Community

This community is centered on the Requests client library and a connected set of HTTP test entities covering Digest authentication, redirects, response handling, and socket-level utilities. The largest cluster concerns HTTP Digest Authentication: test handlers issue 401 challenges through WWW-Authenticate headers, provide nonce and opaque values, receive Digest Authorization headers, and verify credential behavior across redirects and repeated challenges. A second cluster validates redirect processing, including RFC 1808 network-path redirects to non-ASCII locations, fragment propagation across multiple 302 responses, and final 200 responses. Supporting socket handlers test incomplete chunked responses and conflicting Content-Length headers. The evidence indicates a technically focused validation ecosystem for authentication safety, redirect correctness, response parsing, and error handling rather than a community associated with claims of wrongdoing.

## Digest authentication is the community's primary technical focus

HTTP Digest Authentication is the central capability cluster, linking authentication challenges, successful 200 responses, 401 Unauthorized responses, and tests for repeated or improperly triggered authentication. The test suite models an authentication flow in which an unauthenticated request receives a challenge and the client later returns credentials in an Authorization header [Data: Entities (362, 365, 366); Relationships (529, 534, 536, 530, 532)].

The evidence specifically describes challenge processing through nonce, opaque, realm, and quality-of-protection parameters. This makes the cluster relevant to assessing whether the client implements HTTP authentication state transitions correctly [Data: Entities (368, 372, 373); Relationships (538, 539, 537)].

## Credential handling is tested at the request-header level

The community includes an explicit Digest Authorization request entity connected to the Authorization header and the test account named user. This indicates that the tests inspect the structure and identity associated with credentials sent by the client [Data: Entities (369, 370, 374); Relationships (540, 541)].

The authentication challenge includes a server-provided nonce and opaque value, which are inputs to the Digest exchange. The supplied records therefore support a detailed focus on whether authentication material is generated and transmitted in the expected HTTP fields [Data: Entities (368, 372, 373); Relationships (538, 539)].

## Redirect isolation is an important security behavior

The Digest response handler validates authentication during a redirect sequence and confirms that credentials are withheld when a request moves to a different host. It then authenticates the final request only when credentials are appropriately supplied [Data: Entities (375); Relationships (543)].

A dedicated redirect test covers a successful Digest exchange, a 302 redirect, credential isolation on the redirected host, and a final 200 response. These records make redirect handling significant not merely for navigation correctness, but also for preventing inappropriate credential reuse across hosts [Data: Entities (377); Relationships (549)].

## The suite limits authentication retries and triggers

The DIGESTAUTH 401 ONLY SENT ONCE test verifies that the client responds to an initial Digest challenge but does not answer a second consecutive 401 challenge. The corresponding failed-response handler sends two successive 401 responses to exercise this retry limit [Data: Entities (363, 376, 378); Relationships (530, 547, 551)].

A separate test verifies that Digest credentials are not sent when a 200 OK response contains a WWW-Authenticate header. This distinguishes a genuine 4xx authentication challenge from a misleading header on a successful response [Data: Entities (364, 379); Relationships (532, 552)].

## Redirect processing covers non-ASCII locations

The RFC 1808 redirect test uses Requests to follow a network-path redirect containing a non-ASCII path and validates the resulting encoded URL. The associated response handler sends a 301 redirect and then returns a successful response after the redirected request [Data: Entities (387, 390); Relationships (567, 569, 571)].

The test also asserts that the final redirected response has status code 200. This establishes a focused compatibility check for URL encoding and successful navigation after a permanent redirect [Data: Entities (394); Relationships (570)].

## Fragment propagation across redirects is explicitly validated

The fragment-update test uses Requests to follow redirects and verify fragment propagation rules. Its handler processes two sequential 302 responses, first introducing a relevant-section fragment and then redirecting to a fragment-free final URL before returning a 200 response [Data: Entities (389, 391); Relationships (575, 577, 578)].

The connected HTTP 302 Redirect entity represents temporary redirects used to change the request path and fragment across multiple requests. This demonstrates that the community tests not only status-code following, but also preservation and replacement of URL fragments during redirect chains [Data: Entities (393); Relationships (577, 578)].

The consume_socket_content utility reads request data from a socket, optionally with a timeout, so response handlers can inspect incoming HTTP requests. It is connected to an echo response handler and is used before malformed-response handlers send their test responses [Data: Entities (348); Relationships (514, 515, 516)].

    stop responding if challenged again.

    text_401 = (b'HTTP/1.1 401 UNAUTHORIZED\r\n'

                b'WWW-Authenticate: Digest nonce="6bf5d6e4da1ce66918800195d6b9130d"'
                b', opaque="372825293d1c26955496c80ed6426e9e", '
                b'realm="me@kennethreitz.com", qop=auth\r\n\r\n')

    expected_digest = (b'Authorization: Digest username="user", '
                       b'realm="me@kennethreitz.com", '
                       b'nonce="6bf5d6e4da1ce66918800195d6b9130d", uri="/"')

    auth = requests.auth.HTTPDigestAuth('user', 'pass')

    def digest_failed_response_handler(sock):
        # Respond to initial GET with a challenge.
        request_content = consume_socket_content(sock, timeout=0.5)
        assert request_content.startswith(b"GET / HTTP/1.1")
        sock.send(text_401)

        # Verify we receive an Authorization header in response, then
        # challenge again.
        request_content = consume_socket_content(sock, timeout=0.5)
        assert expected_digest in request_content
        sock.send(text_401)

        # Verify the client didn't respond to second challenge.
        request_content = consume_socket_content(sock, timeout=0.5)
        assert request_content == b''

    close_server = threading.Event()
    server = Server(digest_failed_response_handler, wait_to_close_event=close_server)

        close_server.set()

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

So, we can access the headers using any capitalization we want::

    >>> r.headers['Content-Type']
    'application/json'

    >>> r.headers.get('content-type')
    'application/json'

It is also special in that the server could have sent the same header multiple
times with different values, but requests combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

    A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name
    into one "field-name: field-value" pair, without changing the semantics
    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

Cookies
-------

If a response contains some Cookies, you can quickly access them::

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'
    >>> r = requests.get(url)

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']
    'example_cookie_value'

To send your own cookies to the server, you can use the ``cookies``
parameter::

    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> cookies = dict(cookies_are='working')

    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=cookies)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"cookies_are": "working"}}'

Cookies are returned in a :class:`~requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar`,
which acts like a ``dict`` but also offers a more complete interface,
suitable for use over multiple domains or paths.  Cookie jars can
also be passed in to requests::

    >>> jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar()
    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')
    >>> jar.set('gross_cookie', 'blech', domain='httpbin.org', path='/elsewhere')
    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'


Redirection and History
-----------------------

By default Requests will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

We can use the ``history`` property of the Response object to track redirection.

The :attr:`Response.history <requests.Response.history>` list contains the
:class:`Response <requests.Response>` objects that were created in order to
complete the request. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent
response.

For example, GitHub redirects all HTTP requests to HTTPS::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/')

    >>> r.url
    'https://github.com/'

    >>> r.status_code
    200

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


If you're using GET, OPTIONS, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, you can disable
redirection handling with the ``allow_redirects`` parameter::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=False)

    >>> r.status_code
    301

    >>> r.history
    []

If you're using HEAD, you can enable redirection as well::

    >>> r = requests.head('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=True)

    >>> r.url
    'https://github.com/'

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


Timeouts
--------

You can tell Requests to stop waiting for a response after a given number of
seconds with the ``timeout`` parameter. Nearly all production code should use
this parameter in nearly all requests. Failure to do so can cause your program
to hang indefinitely::

    >>> requests.get('https://github.com/', timeout=0.001)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
    requests.exceptions.Timeout: HTTPConnectionPool(host='github.com', port=80): Request timed out. (timeout=0.001)


.. admonition:: Note

    ``timeout`` is not a time limit on the entire response download;
    rather, an exception is raised if the server has not issued a
    response for ``timeout`` seconds (more precisely, if no bytes have been
    received on the underlying socket for ``timeout`` seconds). If no timeout is specified explicitly, requests do
    not time out.


Errors and Exceptions
---------------------

In the event of a network problem (e.g. DNS failure, refused connection, etc),
Requests will raise a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` exception.

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>` will
raise an :exc:`~requests.exceptions.HTTPError` if the HTTP request
returned an unsuccessful status code.

If a request times out, a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.Timeout` exception is
raised.

If a request exceeds the configured number of maximum redirections, a
:exc:`~requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception is raised.

# Requests HTTP Authentication and Redirect Test Community

This community is centered on the Requests client library and a connected set of HTTP test entities covering Digest authentication, redirects, response handling, and socket-level utilities. The largest cluster concerns HTTP Digest Authentication: test handlers issue 401 challenges through WWW-Authenticate headers, provide nonce and opaque values, receive Digest Authorization headers, and verify credential behavior across redirects and repeated challenges. A second cluster validates redirect processing, including RFC 1808 network-path redirects to non-ASCII locations, fragment propagation across multiple 302 responses, and final 200 responses. Supporting socket handlers test incomplete chunked responses and conflicting Content-Length headers. The evidence indicates a technically focused validation ecosystem for authentication safety, redirect correctness, response parsing, and error handling rather than a community associated with claims of wrongdoing.

## Digest authentication is the community's primary technical focus

HTTP Digest Authentication is the central capability cluster, linking authentication challenges, successful 200 responses, 401 Unauthorized responses, and tests for repeated or improperly triggered authentication. The test suite models an authentication flow in which an unauthenticated request receives a challenge and the client later returns credentials in an Authorization header [Data: Entities (362, 365, 366); Relationships (529, 534, 536, 530, 532)].

The evidence specifically describes challenge processing through nonce, opaque, realm, and quality-of-protection parameters. This makes the cluster relevant to assessing whether the client implements HTTP authentication state transitions correctly [Data: Entities (368, 372, 373); Relationships (538, 539, 537)].

## Credential handling is tested at the request-header level

The community includes an explicit Digest Authorization request entity connected to the Authorization header and the test account named user. This indicates that the tests inspect the structure and identity associated with credentials sent by the client [Data: Entities (369, 370, 374); Relationships (540, 541)].

The authentication challenge includes a server-provided nonce and opaque value, which are inputs to the Digest exchange. The supplied records therefore support a detailed focus on whether authentication material is generated and transmitted in the expected HTTP fields [Data: Entities (368, 372, 373); Relationships (538, 539)].

## Redirect isolation is an important security behavior

The Digest response handler validates authentication during a redirect sequence and confirms that credentials are withheld when a request moves to a different host. It then authenticates the final request only when credentials are appropriately supplied [Data: Entities (375); Relationships (543)].

A dedicated redirect test covers a successful Digest exchange, a 302 redirect, credential isolation on the redirected host, and a final 200 response. These records make redirect handling significant not merely for navigation correctness, but also for preventing inappropriate credential reuse across hosts [Data: Entities (377); Relationships (549)].

## The suite limits authentication retries and triggers

The DIGESTAUTH 401 ONLY SENT ONCE test verifies that the client responds to an initial Digest challenge but does not answer a second consecutive 401 challenge. The corresponding failed-response handler sends two successive 401 responses to exercise this retry limit [Data: Entities (363, 376, 378); Relationships (530, 547, 551)].

A separate test verifies that Digest credentials are not sent when a 200 OK response contains a WWW-Authenticate header. This distinguishes a genuine 4xx authentication challenge from a misleading header on a successful response [Data: Entities (364, 379); Relationships (532, 552)].

## Redirect processing covers non-ASCII locations

The RFC 1808 redirect test uses Requests to follow a network-path redirect containing a non-ASCII path and validates the resulting encoded URL. The associated response handler sends a 301 redirect and then returns a successful response after the redirected request [Data: Entities (387, 390); Relationships (567, 569, 571)].

The test also asserts that the final redirected response has status code 200. This establishes a focused compatibility check for URL encoding and successful navigation after a permanent redirect [Data: Entities (394); Relationships (570)].

## Fragment propagation across redirects is explicitly validated

The fragment-update test uses Requests to follow redirects and verify fragment propagation rules. Its handler processes two sequential 302 responses, first introducing a relevant-section fragment and then redirecting to a fragment-free final URL before returning a 200 response [Data: Entities (389, 391); Relationships (575, 577, 578)].

The connected HTTP 302 Redirect entity represents temporary redirects used to change the request path and fragment across multiple requests. This demonstrates that the community tests not only status-code following, but also preservation and replacement of URL fragments during redirect chains [Data: Entities (393); Relationships (577, 578)].

## Socket utilities support malformed-response and request-inspection tests

The consume_socket_content utility reads request data from a socket, optionally with a timeout, so response handlers can inspect incoming HTTP requests. It is connected to an echo response handler and is used before malformed-response handlers send their test responses [Data: Entities (348); Relationships (514, 515, 516)].

The related handlers test an incomplete chunked response that lacks valid terminating chunks and a response with conflicting Content-Length headers. These entities indicate coverage of parser and response-validation failure modes, although the supplied evidence does not state the resulting client behavior beyond the purpose of the tests [Data: Entities (351, 352); Relationships (515, 516)].

## The community is organized as a cohesive local HTTP test environment

Multiple entities describe local test-server handlers that receive requests, issue redirects or authentication challenges, and return final responses. The Digest response handler, redirect response handler, and fragment response handler each connect request-processing behavior to specific HTTP status responses [Data: Entities (375, 390, 391); Relationships (543, 547, 571, 578)].

The resulting structure links client behavior, socket-level server utilities, HTTP status entities, headers, authentication parameters, and test events. Based on the supplied records, the community's significance is its breadth of protocol validation across authentication, redirects, URL handling, and malformed responses [Data: Relationships (514, 529, 534, 567, 575)].

class Response:
    """The :class:`Response <Response>` object, which contains a
    server's response to an HTTP request.
    """

    __attrs__ = [
        "_content",
        "status_code",
        "headers",
        "url",
        "history",
        "encoding",
        "reason",
        "cookies",
        "elapsed",
        "request",
    ]

    def __init__(self):
        self._content = False
        self._content_consumed = False
        self._next = None

        #: Integer Code of responded HTTP Status, e.g. 404 or 200.
        self.status_code = None

        #: Case-insensitive Dictionary of Response Headers.
        #: For example, ``headers['content-encoding']`` will return the
        #: value of a ``'Content-Encoding'`` response header.
        self.headers = CaseInsensitiveDict()

        #: File-like object representation of response (for advanced usage).
        #: Use of ``raw`` requires that ``stream=True`` be set on the request.
        #: This requirement does not apply for use internally to Requests.
        self.raw = None

        #: Final URL location of Response.
        self.url = None

        #: Encoding to decode with when accessing r.text.
        self.encoding = None

        #: A list of :class:`Response <Response>` objects from
        #: the history of the Request. Any redirect responses will end
        #: up here. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent request.
        self.history = []

        #: Textual reason of responded HTTP Status, e.g. "Not Found" or "OK".
        self.reason = None

        #: A CookieJar of Cookies the server sent back.
        self.cookies = cookiejar_from_dict({})

        #: The amount of time elapsed between sending the request
        #: and the arrival of the response (as a timedelta).
        #: This property specifically measures the time taken between sending
        #: the first byte of the request and finishing parsing the headers. It
        #: is therefore unaffected by consuming the response content or the
        #: value of the ``stream`` keyword argument.
        self.elapsed = datetime.timedelta(0)

        #: The :class:`PreparedRequest <PreparedRequest>` object to which this
        #: is a response.
        self.request = None

    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *args):
        self.close()

    def __getstate__(self):

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

So, we can access the headers using any capitalization we want::

    >>> r.headers['Content-Type']
    'application/json'

    >>> r.headers.get('content-type')
    'application/json'

It is also special in that the server could have sent the same header multiple
times with different values, but requests combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

    A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name
    into one ""field-name: field-value"" pair, without changing the semantics
    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

Cookies
-------

If a response contains some Cookies, you can quickly access them::

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'
    >>> r = requests.get(url)

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']
    'example_cookie_value'

To send your own cookies to the server, you can use the ``cookies``
parameter::

    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> cookies = dict(cookies_are='working')

    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=cookies)
    >>> r.text
    '{""cookies"": {""cookies_are"": ""working""}}'

Cookies are returned in a :class:`~requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar`,
which acts like a ``dict`` but also offers a more complete interface,
suitable for use over multiple domains or paths.  Cookie jars can
also be passed in to requests::

    >>> jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar()
    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')
    >>> jar.set('gross_cookie', 'blech', domain='httpbin.org', path='/elsewhere')
    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{""cookies"": {""tasty_cookie"": ""yum""}}'


Redirection and History
-----------------------

By default Requests will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

We can use the ``history`` property of the Response object to track redirection.

The :attr:`Response.history <requests.Response.history>` list contains the
:class:`Response <requests.Response>` objects that were created in order to
complete the request. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent
response.

For example, GitHub redirects all HTTP requests to HTTPS::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/')

    >>> r.url
    'https://github.com/'

    >>> r.status_code
    200

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


If you're using GET, OPTIONS, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, you can disable
redirection handling with the ``allow_redirects`` parameter::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=False)

    >>> r.status_code
    301

    >>> r.history
    []

If you're using HEAD, you can enable redirection as well::

    >>> r = requests.head('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=True)

    >>> r.url
    'https://github.com/'

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


Timeouts
--------

You can tell Requests to stop waiting for a response after a given number of
seconds with the ``timeout`` parameter. Nearly all production code should use
this parameter in nearly all requests. Failure to do so can cause your program
to hang indefinitely::

    >>> requests.get('https://github.com/', timeout=0.001)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File ""<stdin>"", line 1, in <module>
    requests.exceptions.Timeout: HTTPConnectionPool(host='github.com', port=80): Request timed out. (timeout=0.001)


.. admonition:: Note

    ``timeout`` is not a time limit on the entire response download;
    rather, an exception is raised if the server has not issued a
    response for ``timeout`` seconds (more precisely, if no bytes have been
    received on the underlying socket for ``timeout`` seconds). If no timeout is specified explicitly, requests do
    not time out.


Errors and Exceptions
---------------------

In the event of a network problem (e.g. DNS failure, refused connection, etc),
Requests will raise a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` exception.

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>` will
raise an :exc:`~requests.exceptions.HTTPError` if the HTTP request
returned an unsuccessful status code.

If a request times out, a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.Timeout` exception is
raised.

If a request exceeds the configured number of maximum redirections, a
:exc:`~requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception is raised.

# Requests HTTP Authentication and Redirect Test Community

This community is centered on the Requests client library and a connected set of HTTP test entities covering Digest authentication, redirects, response handling, and socket-level utilities. The largest cluster concerns HTTP Digest Authentication: test handlers issue 401 challenges through WWW-Authenticate headers, provide nonce and opaque values, receive Digest Authorization headers, and verify credential behavior across redirects and repeated challenges. A second cluster validates redirect processing, including RFC 1808 network-path redirects to non-ASCII locations, fragment propagation across multiple 302 responses, and final 200 responses. Supporting socket handlers test incomplete chunked responses and conflicting Content-Length headers. The evidence indicates a technically focused validation ecosystem for authentication safety, redirect correctness, response parsing, and error handling rather than a community associated with claims of wrongdoing.

## Digest authentication is the community's primary technical focus

HTTP Digest Authentication is the central capability cluster, linking authentication challenges, successful 200 responses, 401 Unauthorized responses, and tests for repeated or improperly triggered authentication. The test suite models an authentication flow in which an unauthenticated request receives a challenge and the client later returns credentials in an Authorization header [Data: Entities (362, 365, 366); Relationships (529, 534, 536, 530, 532)].

The evidence specifically describes challenge processing through nonce, opaque, realm, and quality-of-protection parameters. This makes the cluster relevant to assessing whether the client implements HTTP authentication state transitions correctly [Data: Entities (368, 372, 373); Relationships (538, 539, 537)].

## Credential handling is tested at the request-header level

The community includes an explicit Digest Authorization request entity connected to the Authorization header and the test account named user. This indicates that the tests inspect the structure and identity associated with credentials sent by the client [Data: Entities (369, 370, 374); Relationships (540, 541)].

The authentication challenge includes a server-provided nonce and opaque value, which are inputs to the Digest exchange. The supplied records therefore support a detailed focus on whether authentication material is generated and transmitted in the expected HTTP fields [Data: Entities (368, 372, 373); Relationships (538, 539)].

## Redirect isolation is an important security behavior

The Digest response handler validates authentication during a redirect sequence and confirms that credentials are withheld when a request moves to a different host. It then authenticates the final request only when credentials are appropriately supplied [Data: Entities (375); Relationships (543)].

A dedicated redirect test covers a successful Digest exchange, a 302 redirect, credential isolation on the redirected host, and a final 200 response. These records make redirect handling significant not merely for navigation correctness, but also for preventing inappropriate credential reuse across hosts [Data: Entities (377); Relationships (549)].

## The suite limits authentication retries and triggers

The DIGESTAUTH 401 ONLY SENT ONCE test verifies that the client responds to an initial Digest challenge but does not answer a second consecutive 401 challenge. The corresponding failed-response handler sends two successive 401 responses to exercise this retry limit [Data: Entities (363, 376, 378); Relationships (530, 547, 551)].

A separate test verifies that Digest credentials are not sent when a 200 OK response contains a WWW-Authenticate header. This distinguishes a genuine 4xx authentication challenge from a misleading header on a successful response [Data: Entities (364, 379); Relationships (532, 552)].

## Redirect processing covers non-ASCII locations

The RFC 1808 redirect test uses Requests to follow a network-path redirect containing a non-ASCII path and validates the resulting encoded URL. The associated response handler sends a 301 redirect and then returns a successful response after the redirected request [Data: Entities (387, 390); Relationships (567, 569, 571)].

The test also asserts that the final redirected response has status code 200. This establishes a focused compatibility check for URL encoding and successful navigation after a permanent redirect [Data: Entities (394); Relationships (570)].

## Fragment propagation across redirects is explicitly validated

The fragment-update test uses Requests to follow redirects and verify fragment propagation rules. Its handler processes two sequential 302 responses, first introducing a relevant-section fragment and then redirecting to a fragment-free final URL before returning a 200 response [Data: Entities (389, 391); Relationships (575, 577, 578)].

The connected HTTP 302 Redirect entity represents temporary redirects used to change the request path and fragment across multiple requests. This demonstrates that the community tests not only status-code following, but also preservation and replacement of URL fragments during redirect chains [Data: Entities (393); Relationships (577, 578)].

## Socket utilities support malformed-response and request-inspection tests

The consume_socket_content utility reads request data from a socket, optionally with a timeout, so response handlers can inspect incoming HTTP requests. It is connected to an echo response handler and is used before malformed-response handlers send their test responses [Data: Entities (348); Relationships (514, 515, 516)].

The related handlers test an incomplete chunked response that lacks valid terminating chunks and a response with conflicting Content-Length headers. These entities indicate coverage of parser and response-validation failure modes, although the supplied evidence does not state the resulting client behavior beyond the purpose of the tests [Data: Entities (351, 352); Relationships (515, 516)].

## The community is organized as a cohesive local HTTP test environment

Multiple entities describe local test-server handlers that receive requests, issue redirects or authentication challenges, and return final responses. The Digest response handler, redirect response handler, and fragment response handler each connect request-processing behavior to specific HTTP status responses [Data: Entities (375, 390, 391); Relationships (543, 547, 571, 578)].

The resulting structure links client behavior, socket-level server utilities, HTTP status entities, headers, authentication parameters, and test events. Based on the supplied records, the community's significance is its breadth of protocol validation across authentication, redirects, URL handling, and malformed responses [Data: Relationships (514, 529, 534, 567, 575)].

Cookies
-------

If a response contains some Cookies, you can quickly access them::

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'
    >>> r = requests.get(url)

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']
    'example_cookie_value'

To send your own cookies to the server, you can use the ``cookies``
parameter::

    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> cookies = dict(cookies_are='working')

    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=cookies)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"cookies_are": "working"}}'

Cookies are returned in a :class:`~requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar`,
which acts like a ``dict`` but also offers a more complete interface,
suitable for use over multiple domains or paths.  Cookie jars can
also be passed in to requests::

    >>> jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar()
    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')
    >>> jar.set('gross_cookie', 'blech', domain='httpbin.org', path='/elsewhere')
    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'


Redirection and History
-----------------------

By default Requests will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

We can use the ``history`` property of the Response object to track redirection.

The :attr:`Response.history <requests.Response.history>` list contains the
:class:`Response <requests.Response>` objects that were created in order to
complete the request. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent
response.

For example, GitHub redirects all HTTP requests to HTTPS::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/')

    >>> r.url
    'https://github.com/'

    >>> r.status_code
    200

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


If you're using GET, OPTIONS, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, you can disable
redirection handling with the ``allow_redirects`` parameter::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=False)

    >>> r.status_code
    301

    >>> r.history
    []

If you're using HEAD, you can enable redirection as well::

    >>> r = requests.head('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=True)

    >>> r.url
    'https://github.com/'

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


Timeouts
--------

You can tell Requests to stop waiting for a response after a given number of
seconds with the ``timeout`` parameter. Nearly all production code should use
this parameter in nearly all requests. Failure to do so can cause your program
to hang indefinitely::

    >>> requests.get('https://github.com/', timeout=0.001)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
    requests.exceptions.Timeout: HTTPConnectionPool(host='github.com', port=80): Request timed out. (timeout=0.001)


.. admonition:: Note

    ``timeout`` is not a time limit on the entire response download;
    rather, an exception is raised if the server has not issued a
    response for ``timeout`` seconds (more precisely, if no bytes have been
    received on the underlying socket for ``timeout`` seconds). If no timeout is specified explicitly, requests do
    not time out.


Errors and Exceptions
---------------------

In the event of a network problem (e.g. DNS failure, refused connection, etc),
Requests will raise a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` exception.

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>` will
raise an :exc:`~requests.exceptions.HTTPError` if the HTTP request
returned an unsuccessful status code.

If a request times out, a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.Timeout` exception is
raised.

If a request exceeds the configured number of maximum redirections, a
:exc:`~requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception is raised.
